assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the Go team's own guidance (Effective Go / spec, cited by the guide): panic is for truly exceptional internal failure, errors are the ordinary mechanism. No change in 1.26/1.27.
assertions_contracts.evidence: Guide cites the Go specification and Effective Go; neither changed on this point.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: No assertion statement in Go: explicit invariant checks in code and tests; panic reserved for broken programmer contracts or irrecoverable internal state; never panic on malformed external data; no recover to fake success; compile-time interface checks do not validate external data.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official Go source prescribes budgets; nothing contradicts bounded admission. 1.27's runtime work (size-specialized allocation) reduces allocation cost but does not bound anything for the application.
bounded_work.evidence: Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design; no contradicting official position in the 1.27 announcement or release history.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named Max constants for input bytes, items, nesting depth, workers, queue entries, retries and output capture; no goroutine per unbounded input item (bounded workers with admission); no unbounded io.ReadAll (limited reader plus max+1 check); retries need idempotence, shared deadline, bounded backoff.

concurrency.best_practice: The ownership discipline holds, but 1.27 made the goroutineleak profile in runtime/pprof generally available - an official, GC-based detector for permanently blocked goroutines - which is the standard tool for the exact failure class (goroutine leaks) the guide polices purely by construction discipline.
concurrency.evidence: The official Go 1.27 announcement lists goroutine leak profiles among its headline additions; the 1.27.1/1.27.2 minor revisions in the official release history keep the feature current.
concurrency.guide_position: Contexts signal cancellation but do not kill goroutines; every worker has a shutdown path and an owner that waits; sender closes owned channels exactly once; one owner for shared state or a mutex/atomic protocol; happens-before via mutexes/channels/atomics; race detector noted as not a proof.

error_handling.best_practice: Fully aligned with official Go practice (errors are values, wrap for Is/As). 1.27 strengthens the guide's 'never compare message strings' rule in practice: encoding/json is now implemented on the v2 engine, behaviour is preserved but the exact text of some error messages differs - code that compared strings is exactly what breaks.
error_handling.evidence: Go 1.27 announcement lists the encoding/json/v2 package as a headline change; release-notes coverage of the v2 backing notes preserved behaviour with possibly different error text, and a temporary GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 opt-out.
error_handling.guide_position: Return (value, error) consistently; wrap with %w for errors.Is/As; never compare message strings; handle Close errors; a typed nil in an error interface is not nil; never panic on malformed external data.

formatting.best_practice: Unchanged through 1.27: gofmt output is canonical, and go fix (expanded in 1.26/1.27 with new modernizers) is the sanctioned mechanical-upgrade path, complementary to - not a replacement for - gofmt.
formatting.evidence: Guide cites Effective Go/formatting; 1.27 tooling notes add go fix modernizers without altering gofmt authority.
formatting.guide_position: gofmt is authoritative including its tabs; never force spaces or a hard 100-column wrap onto gofmt output; keep lines readable through function design; one reviewed import organizer (goimports in the skill pairing).

memory_ownership.best_practice: Guidance remains correct; 1.27's size-specialized allocation (cheaper small allocations) is a runtime improvement and does not change ownership/retention obligations.
memory_ownership.evidence: 1.27 announcement lists faster memory allocation among its highlights; nothing in it revises slice-aliasing or Pool semantics the guide states.
memory_ownership.guide_position: GC does not bound queues or prevent leaks; cap workers/channels/maps/bodies/pools; a small subslice can retain a large backing array (clone a small retained result); sync.Pool is a reuse optimization, not storage or a capacity guarantee; check sizes before make.

security.best_practice: Core guidance holds - the os.Root traversal-resistant APIs the guide recommends remain current (and its Section 19 correctly notes os.Root is not a sandbox for device files/proc/mounts). The dependency-vulnerability half of security is scored under static_analysis (govulncheck gap).
security.evidence: Guide cites the Go team's osroot blog post itself; no deprecation of os.Root through 1.27 was found in the sources fetched.
security.guide_position: Treat unsafe, cgo, reflection, plugins and build directives as trust boundaries; bound HTTP headers/bodies, set timeouts, verify TLS; no pprof/debug endpoints on untrusted interfaces; SSRF care; os.OpenRoot descriptor-relative traversal policy instead of prefix checks; secrets out of errors/logs.

static_analysis.best_practice: The official gate is wider than the guide's: govulncheck (the Go team's vulnerability scanner, golang.org/x/vuln) reports only vulnerabilities in code actually called, using the Go vulnerability database, and is the standard CI security gate for Go modules. The guide's validation recipe (vet, test, test -race, bench) never runs it, and its dependency section mentions checksum review only.
static_analysis.evidence: govulncheck's official package documentation describes the call-graph-based scanner maintained by the Go team; it has been the recommended tool since long before the guide's 2026-09-23 source review, which omits it.
static_analysis.guide_position: go vet in the validation recipe; review go.mod/go.sum, replacements and toolchain directives; checksums verify content, not suitability; audit go generate; no vulnerability-database scan is prescribed anywhere.

testing.best_practice: testing/synctest graduated from experiment (1.24) to general availability in Go 1.25: tests run in a bubble with a fake clock that advances only when all goroutines are durably blocked, making timeout/cancellation tests deterministic and fast without sleeps - the guide prescribes the goal but not the tool. 1.27 adds synctest.Sleep on top.
testing.evidence: The Go team's synctest blog post states the package graduated to general availability in Go 1.25; the guide's sources were reviewed 2026-09-23, after graduation, and still omit it.
testing.guide_position: Table-driven boundary tests and fuzz targets for parsers; cancellation before/during work, full queues, closed channels, blocked peers, partial I/O, shutdown joins; race tests on concurrent paths; 'do not depend on sleeps: use synchronization or a controlled clock'.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: Go's release policy supports each major release only until two newer majors exist. Go 1.27.0 shipped 2026-08-19 and 1.27.2 on 2026-10-08, so the only supported majors are 1.27 and 1.26; 1.24 lost support when 1.26 shipped in February 2026. A 1.24+ primary target now names an unsupported toolchain as the baseline.
toolchain_pins.evidence: Official release-history page states the two-newer-releases support policy and lists go1.27.0 (2026-08-19) and go1.27.2 (2026-10-08, including security fixes).
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Header: 'Primary target: Go 1.24+'; Section 2: Go 1.24 is the guide's minimum because of the os.Root APIs; GOTOOLCHAIN=local guidance for CI; module/toolchain versions recorded explicitly.

current_versions.delve (dlv): Still the standard Go DAP debugger; pairing holds
current_versions.go: 1.27.2 (2026-10-08) is the latest patch; 1.27.0 released 2026-08-19 with generic methods, encoding/json/v2 in the stdlib, a uuid package, goroutine leak profiles and faster allocation; supported majors are only 1.27 and 1.26
current_versions.gofmt/goimports: gofmt unchanged and authoritative; goimports still the standard import organizer in golang.org/x/tools
current_versions.gopls: Official Go language server (Go team, golang.org/x/tools/gopls), versioned independently of the Go release; pairing holds - the 'gop_ls' string in SKILL.md is a different (Go+/XGo) server name
current_versions.govulncheck: Official Go vulnerability scanner (golang.org/x/vuln), call-graph based; absent from the guide's gates
current_versions.staticcheck: Community (Honnef) analyzer, not an official Go tool; guide does not name it - no stale claim to correct

mechanical_fixes.correct: **Primary target:** Go 1.27+ (1.26 supported); module and toolchain versions recorded explicitly
mechanical_fixes.current: **Primary target:** Go 1.24+; module and toolchain versions recorded explicitly
mechanical_fixes.evidence: Go's official release policy supports a major release only until two newer majors exist; with 1.27.0 released 2026-08-19 (latest patch 1.27.2, 2026-10-08), 1.24 has been unsupported since 1.26 shipped. Note: Section 2's separate statement that os.Root needs 1.24 remains accurate as a feature floor and is not part of this fix.

gop_ls is the language server name for Go+/XGo, not Go; the Go team's official language server is gopls, which the same SKILL.md correctly names in its description, metadata (lsp: gopls) and toolchain pairing line - the compatibility line contradicts the file itself.

proposals.evidence: govulncheck's official documentation describes a scanner that uses static call-graph analysis to report only vulnerabilities in functions the program actually calls, against the Go vulnerability database - precision a checksum review cannot provide.
proposals.proposal: Add govulncheck ./... as a required gate alongside go vet in the validation recipe, with the tool version pinned like other development tools (the guide's own dependency rule).
proposals.recommendation: Adopt - it is the Go team's own tool, low-noise by design, and closes the guide's one clear security-gate gap.

proposals.evidence: The Go team's synctest post states the package graduated to general availability in Go 1.25 with a fake clock that advances only when every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked; Go 1.27 adds synctest.Sleep.
proposals.proposal: Name testing/synctest as the prescribed 'controlled clock' in Section 28: write timeout, deadline and cancellation tests inside synctest bubbles (synctest.Test/Wait) instead of real sleeps or hand-rolled fake clocks, on any module at Go 1.25+.
proposals.recommendation: Adopt for all concurrency tests; keep the sleep ban, now with the standard tool attached to it.

proposals.evidence: The official Go 1.27 announcement lists goroutine leak profiles among the release's headline features, available via runtime/pprof.
proposals.proposal: Add the 1.27 goroutineleak profile to the concurrency review: services should expose/collect the goroutineleak pprof profile in diagnostics, and leak investigations start there before manual stack audits.
proposals.recommendation: Adopt as a diagnostics rule (not an endpoint-exposure change - the guide's warning against public pprof endpoints still applies to where it is served).
